# Eigenvalues and the $\beta$-Ensembles

{{< include /_macros.qmd >}}

Consider again the joint density of an $N\times N$ matrix $M$ from the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (the GOE)
$$
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}(M) &\propto \prod_{k=1}^N \mathbb{P}(M_{kk})\prod_{k<\ell}\mathbb{P}(M_{k\ell}) \propto \prod_{k=1}^N \exp\left(
        -\frac{M_{kk}^2}{4\sigma^2}
    \right)
    \prod_{k<\ell}\exp\left(
        -\frac{M_{k\ell}^2}{2\sigma^2}
    \right).
\end{align*}
$$

With some work, one can isolate the eigenvalues $\lambda = (\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N)$ and find the eigenvalue joint probability density function (jpdf)
$$
\begin{equation}
\rho(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{1}{4\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^N \lambda_j^2\right)\prod_{j<k}|\lambda_k - \lambda_j| . 
\end{equation}
$$
It can be instructive to first derive this jpdf for $2\times 2$ matrices before generalising to larger $N$; refer to [@livan2018introduction] for a clear guide. Extending the same argument to the GUE and GSE yields a similar result, and one can show that the generalised jpdf is
$$
\begin{equation*}
    \rho(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{\beta}{4\sigma^2}\sum_{j=1}^N \lambda_j^2\right)\prod_{j<k}|\lambda_k - \lambda_j|^\beta
\end{equation*}
$$
with $\beta \in \{1, 2, 4\}$ corresponding to the GOE, GUE, and GSE respectively. From a structural point of view, $\beta$ describes the number of independent degrees of freedom in each matrix entry. It also describes the strength of the apparent repulsion between the eigenvalues, as seen through the so-called Vandermonde determinant $\prod_{j<k}|\lambda_k - \lambda_j|^\beta$.

It is now convenient to set the variance $\sigma^2 = 1/N$. Recall that this has the eigenvalues concentrate in the interval $[-2, 2]$. By further considering the identity
$$
\begin{equation*}
\prod_i y_i^\beta = \exp\left ( \beta \sum_i \log y_i \right),
\end{equation*}
$$
the eigenvalue jpdf can be written as
$$
\begin{align*}
    \rho(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N) &\propto \exp \left[-\beta N \left(   
        \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N \frac{\lambda_j^2}{2} - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j<k}\log|\lambda_k - \lambda_j|
    \right)    \right]\\
    &=: \exp\big[ -\beta N H_N(\lambda) \big],
\end{align*}
$$
where $H_N(\lambda)$ can be seen as the energy of the system
$$
\begin{equation*}
    H_N(\lambda) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N \frac{\lambda_j^2}{2} - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j<k}\log|\lambda_k - \lambda_j|.
\end{equation*}
$$

This perspective is from statistical mechanics, where the eigenvalues $\lambda$ are treated as interacting particles whose equilibrium arises from a balance of two competing effects: the confinement $\sum_j \lambda_j^2/2$, and the logarithmic repulsion $\sum_{j<k}\log |\lambda_k - \lambda_j|$. The Dyson index $\beta$ acts as an inverse temperature.

As it stands, the fact that $\lambda$ arise as the eigenvalues of the Gaussian ensembles means that the confining potential is quadratic and $\beta$ is restricted to the values $\beta \in \{1, 2, 4\}$. For other ensembles, e.g.\ the Wishart-Laguerre or the Jacobi ensembles, the confining potential takes a different form, but $\beta$ is still restricted to these three values^[At least for the classical matrix models. There are alternative matrix models [@dumitriu2002matrix] that extend several important ensembles, including the Gaussian ensembles, to all $\beta > 0$.]. However, we can always consider a more general form of the eigenvalue jpdf by introducing a generic potential $V$, with appropriate support, so that the Hamiltonian becomes
$$
\begin{equation*}
    H_N(\lambda) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N V(\lambda_j) - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j<k}\log|\lambda_k - \lambda_j|
\end{equation*}
$$
and we allow all $\beta > 0$. With this, the density $\rho(\lambda) \propto \exp[-\beta N H_N(\lambda)]$ describes the $\beta$-ensembles: an incredibly broad class of ensembles and the primary object of interest on this site.
